Name: Understand the carbon intensity of cloud regions
Guideline: Learn how the Carbon-Free Energy (CFE) percentage metric measures the share of clean energy powering each region's grid on an hourly basis, so this data can inform region choices.
Context: Google provides this data both as a public dashboard and programmatically — via a GitHub repository or a BigQuery public dataset — so the CFE percentage can be pulled directly into your own region-selection tooling rather than checked manually.

Name: Incorporate CFE in your location-selection strategy
Guideline: Favor the cleanest available region for long-running workloads using the region picker's low-CO2 indicator, and enforce the choice with Organization Policy resource-location constraints.
Context: The concrete enforcement mechanism is an Organization Policy resource-location constraint — e.g. `in:us-low-carbon-locations` — which technically blocks resource creation outside the approved low-carbon regions rather than relying on developers remembering to check the picker.

Name: Use time-of-day scheduling
Guideline: Shift flexible, compute-intensive workloads such as training and batch inference to run when the local grid's carbon-free energy share is highest, cutting emissions without sacrificing performance.
Context: Google notes grid carbon intensity can swing significantly within a single day, which is exactly what makes this time-shifting approach effective specifically for non-urgent, compute-intensive tasks like training runs rather than for latency-sensitive workloads.

Name: Architect for energy efficiency by using TPUs
Guideline: Use Tensor Processing Units, purpose-built AI accelerators with higher computation per watt than general-purpose hardware, to cut energy use across training, inference, and cooling.
Context: Google's own framing includes the operational side too: TPU data centers use advanced liquid cooling, and the combination of efficiency plus purpose-built architecture is cited as cutting training time from days to hours, not just cutting energy per computation.

Name: Follow the 4Ms best practices for resource selection
Guideline: Apply the Model, Machine, Mechanization, and Map framework -- efficient models, optimized processors, cloud deployment, and low-carbon regions -- to substantially cut the carbon footprint of ML workloads.
Context: Google gives rough multipliers for each M: sparse models can improve efficiency 3-10x, ML-optimized processors 2-5x, cloud deployment over on-premises 1.4-2x, and running in the cleanest-energy regions 5-10x — the four factors are meant to compound, not be chosen from.

Name: Select efficient AI models
Guideline: Default to the smallest model that meets accuracy requirements, such as a distilled variant, instead of automatically reaching for the largest available model.
Context: Google's concrete example is DistilBERT versus BERT specifically — a distilled model achieving similar performance with meaningfully less computational overhead and faster inference, as the pattern for what "default to the smallest model that meets requirements" looks like in practice.

Name: Use domain-specific, hyper-efficient solutions
Guideline: Prefer specialized, pretrained models built for a narrow domain, such as geospatial or weather forecasting, over general-purpose foundation models, since they need far less compute.
Context: Google names its own concrete examples: Earth AI for geospatial data and WeatherNext for weather forecasting — both cited as needing substantially less compute than general-purpose foundation models for their specific domain task.

Name: Apply appropriate model compression techniques
Guideline: Reduce model size and energy use through pruning, quantization, or knowledge distillation while preserving acceptable accuracy.
Context: Google's concrete quantization example is reducing numeric precision from 32-bit down to 8-bit integers specifically, alongside pruning (removing unnecessary parameters) and knowledge distillation (training a smaller "student" model to mimic a larger "teacher").

Name: Use specialized hardware
Guideline: Run training and inference on accelerators purpose-built for ML rather than general-purpose processors to gain multi-fold improvements in performance per watt.
Context: Google's figure here — 2-5x better performance and energy efficiency versus general-purpose CPUs/GPUs — is specifically cited in the context of training workloads, where the compute intensity makes specialized hardware's efficiency advantage matter most.

Name: Use parameter-efficient fine-tuning
Guideline: Fine-tune large models with techniques like LoRA that freeze most weights and train only small additional layers, cutting the cost and energy of adaptation versus full fine-tuning.
Context: A secondary benefit Google notes: since PEFT methods like LoRA only produce small additional layers rather than a full copy of the model, they also cut the storage footprint of maintaining many fine-tuned variants, not just the compute cost of training each one.

Name: Optimize model training processes
Guideline: Reduce wasted training compute with early stopping once validation performance plateaus, efficient data pipelines that keep accelerators fed, and smarter hyperparameter search such as Bayesian optimization.
Context: The efficiency case for early stopping specifically: once validation performance plateaus, continued training epochs burn compute for diminishing or zero accuracy gain, which is exactly the waste this pattern targets — the same logic Google applies to preferring Bayesian search over exhaustive grid search for hyperparameters.

Name: Improve inference efficiency
Guideline: Batch inference requests for parallel processing and use multi-layer caching, including key-value and semantic caches, to avoid recomputing results.
Context: The tradeoff Google is explicit about: batching multiple inference requests together adds a small amount of latency per individual request, in exchange for meaningfully higher accelerator utilization across the batch as a whole.

Name: Measure and monitor
Guideline: Track token usage, energy consumption, and carbon footprint of AI workloads, and monitor production models for drift so optimizations can be correlated with impact.
Context: Google's concrete tool is Cloud Monitoring for tracking these metrics, plus event annotations that tag when a model change was deployed — so a shift in energy consumption or accuracy can actually be traced back to the specific change that caused it.

Name: Implement carbon-aware scheduling
Guideline: Run resource-intensive ML pipeline jobs in the cleanest available regions and during the times when the local grid has the most carbon-free energy.
Context: The concrete tool for finding "cleanest available regions" is Google's own Carbon Footprint report, which identifies the least carbon-intensive regions directly rather than requiring you to source that data elsewhere.

Name: Optimize data pipelines
Guideline: Use managed data-processing services such as Dataflow or Managed Service for Apache Spark to prepare training data efficiently, so expensive compute isn't left idle waiting on data.
Context: The efficiency case here is specifically about accelerator idle time: if data preparation can't keep pace with an AI training job, expensive GPU/TPU capacity sits idle waiting — which is the specific waste Dataflow or Managed Service for Apache Spark are meant to eliminate by keeping the data pipeline itself efficient.

Name: Embrace MLOps
Guideline: Automate the ML lifecycle so models are continuously monitored, validated, and redeployed only when needed, avoiding unnecessary retraining.
Context: The practical mechanism: continuous validation is what determines whether retraining is actually warranted, replacing a fixed retraining schedule (which wastes compute retraining a model that hasn't meaningfully drifted) with one triggered by measured need.

Name: Use managed services
Guideline: Offload resource management to managed AI platforms that provide built-in hyperparameter tuning and resource optimization, reducing the overhead of running efficient infrastructure yourself.
Context: Google's concrete example of such a managed platform is its Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, cited specifically for providing built-in hyperparameter tuning, model monitoring, and resource optimization as part of the platform rather than infrastructure you'd build and tune yourself.

Name: Use horizontal scaling
Guideline: Scale out by adding instances rather than scaling up a single instance's size, since horizontal scaling distributes load more efficiently and adapts better to variable demand.
Context: Google's concrete mechanism for Compute Engine specifically is managed instance groups, which automatically distribute load across multiple VM instances rather than requiring a single instance to be manually resized as demand changes.

Name: Configure appropriate scaling policies
Guideline: Base autoscaling on custom metrics and thresholds tailored to the application rather than CPU utilization alone, to avoid scaling thrash and overprovisioning.
Context: For GKE workloads specifically, Google frames this as configuring a cluster autoscaling policy tailored to your application's own behavior pattern, rather than relying on the platform's generic default thresholds.

Name: Combine reactive and proactive scaling
Guideline: Pair reactive autoscaling for unpredictable spikes with scheduled autoscaling for known, predictable demand patterns.
Context: Google notes that some of its own services already do part of this automatically: GKE Autopilot and Cloud Run both learn workload patterns over time to optimize provisioning, reducing how much of this reactive/proactive balancing you need to configure by hand.

Name: Design stateless applications
Guideline: Keep session state in an external store, such as Redis, rather than on the compute instance itself, so instances can be added or removed freely during scaling.
Context: Google's concrete recommendation for where to put that externalized state is Memorystore for Redis — the point being any compute instance can then serve any user's request, since no instance is holding state the others don't have access to.

Name: Schedule for low carbon intensity
Guideline: Time batch jobs to run in cleaner regions and during periods of abundant renewable energy, using the Carbon Footprint report to find optimal windows.
Context: This specifically targets batch jobs rather than user-facing workloads: because nobody is waiting in real time for a batch job's result, shifting its timing to a cleaner grid window has effectively zero cost to anyone, unlike delaying an interactive request would.

Name: Use Spot VMs for noncritical workloads
Guideline: Run fault-tolerant, non-critical batch jobs on discounted Spot VM capacity instead of provisioning dedicated resources.
Context: The tradeoff Google is explicit about: Spot VMs are steeply discounted precisely because they can be preempted with little notice, which is exactly why this pattern restricts the recommendation to fault-tolerant, non-critical jobs that can handle an interruption gracefully.

Name: Consolidate and parallelize jobs
Guideline: Group similar jobs into larger batches, for example with Batch, to reduce per-job startup and shutdown overhead and keep infrastructure better utilized.
Context: Google's Batch service is named as handling this automatically end-to-end — provisioning, scheduling, and monitoring the consolidated job — rather than requiring you to build your own batching/queuing logic on top of raw compute instances.

Name: Use managed services
Guideline: Let services like Batch and Dataflow provision and scale resources automatically based on workload volume, eliminating idle capacity.
Context: Google's concrete example is Dataflow specifically: it automatically scales the number of workers based on the data volume actually flowing through the pipeline at any given moment, so you're not paying for workers sized for peak volume when the pipeline is mostly idle.

Name: Match VM machine families to workload requirements
Guideline: Pick the machine family -- general-purpose, compute-, memory-, storage-, or accelerator-optimized -- that best fits the workload's actual resource profile.
Context: Google names the specific families to choose between: E2 for general cost efficiency, C2/C3 for CPU-intensive work, M2/M3 for memory-heavy workloads, and Z3 for storage-intensive applications — plus accelerator-optimized instances for ML/AI specifically.

Name: Upgrade to the latest machine types
Guideline: Move to newer processor generations with better power management and higher performance-per-watt to cut both energy use and task completion time.
Context: Google gives specific figures for its own hardware generations: the C4A processor is cited as 60% more energy-efficient than comparable x86 processors, and C4 VMs as offering 40% higher price-performance than the previous C3 generation.

Name: Leverage the scale-to-zero capability of Cloud Run
Guideline: Deploy intermittent or event-driven services on Cloud Run so they scale down to zero instances when idle, eliminating energy waste from unused capacity.
Context: Google's phrasing is specific: Cloud Run "automatically scales instances to zero when there is no incoming traffic" — meaning genuinely zero running instances during idle periods, not just a reduced minimum, which is what distinguishes this from typical autoscaling floors on other compute options.

Name: Automate resource optimization using GKE
Guideline: Use GKE's bin packing, horizontal and vertical pod autoscaling, and topology-aware scheduling to maximize node utilization and cut wasted energy.
Context: Google's bin-packing detail: the goal is to "maximize the utilization of each node" by scheduling pods tightly onto fewer nodes rather than spreading them thinly across many partially-used ones, which is what lets GKE eventually shut down nodes that would otherwise sit lightly loaded.

Name: Configure carbon-aware scheduling
Guideline: Combine geographic shifting to cleaner regions with temporal shifting to periods of higher renewable availability, guided by real-time grid carbon-intensity data.
Context: This draws on the same underlying dataset as Google's region-selection guidance — the "Carbon free energy for Google Cloud regions" GitHub repository or BigQuery dataset — just applied here to live scheduling decisions rather than a one-time region choice.

Name: Optimize for cold start efficiency
Guideline: Keep disaster-recovery resources turned off or scaled to zero, use serverless failover, and automate recovery via infrastructure-as-code instead of maintaining always-on warm standby capacity.
Context: Google's concrete tooling: Terraform (or similar infrastructure-as-code) to provision DR resources only when an actual failover is triggered, with Cloud Run specifically named as one option that can sit at zero cost until it's actually needed.

Name: Balance redundancy and utilization
Guideline: Prefer active-active architectures over active-passive, and replicate data only when genuinely required, so redundant systems don't sit idle wasting energy.
Context: Google's framing is specific: in an active-active setup, "all provisioned resources across both regions actively serve traffic" — meaning nothing is purely standing by as a backup that only gets used during a failover, which is where the waste in active-passive architectures typically comes from.

Name: Eliminate redundant logic and feature bloat
Guideline: Implement only the functionality that provides measurable user value, and regularly audit applications to find and remove features that add computational overhead without real benefit.
Context: Google frames "feature bloat" as the specific anti-pattern this targets — not just avoiding waste in new code, but treating an ongoing audit for already-shipped features that quietly accumulated computational overhead as part of the practice, not a one-time cleanup.

Name: Refactor
Guideline: Periodically revisit and simplify code that has accumulated unused branches or dead paths, rather than letting inefficiencies persist indefinitely.
Context: Google frames this as needing a recurring cadence rather than a one-off cleanup: code that was efficient when written tends to accumulate unused branches and dead paths as requirements shift, so the audit needs to repeat, not just happen once at launch.

Name: Avoid unnecessary operations
Guideline: Defer computation until a result is actually needed, using techniques like lazy evaluation so unused work is never performed.
Context: The specific case this targets: a value that gets computed but then never actually gets used because of an early exit or conditional branch — lazy evaluation defers the work until something actually asks for the result, so that unused-value scenario costs nothing.

Name: Prioritize code readability and reusability
Guideline: Follow the DRY principle and write clear, reusable code to minimize duplicated logic, which also reduces the effort -- and associated emissions -- of ongoing development and maintenance.
Context: This one is a different kind of saving than most guidelines on this list: the emissions reduction here comes from less duplicated logic to maintain and review over the codebase's lifetime, not from the running program itself using less energy per execution.

Name: Cache frequent data
Guideline: Keep frequently accessed data in a fast, temporary store such as Memorystore to cut down on repeated database queries and disk I/O.
Context: This is the general pattern that the next several guidelines each specialize — caching API responses, preferring in-memory storage, choosing a write strategy, and picking an eviction policy are all refinements of this same core idea: hold hot data somewhere faster than the database.

Name: Cache API responses
Guideline: Cache the results of frequent API calls to avoid repeating the same costly network requests and computation.
Context: Distinct from general data caching, this specifically targets external network calls — an API response cached locally avoids repeating not just the compute on the far end, but the network round-trip and its associated energy cost too.

Name: Prioritize in-memory caching
Guideline: Favor high-speed RAM-based caches over persistent storage to sidestep slow disk I/O and complex database lookups.
Context: The two costs this specifically sidesteps: slow disk I/O and the computational overhead of a database query planner, both of which a RAM-based cache bypasses entirely by returning data that's already sitting in memory.

Name: Select appropriate cache-write strategies
Guideline: Choose write-through caching to boost cache-hit rates and cut reads, or write-back caching for write-heavy workloads to reduce immediate database load.
Context: The deciding factor Google names: whether your workload is read-heavy (favoring write-through, which keeps the cache always current at write time) or write-heavy (favoring write-back, which defers the persistent-store write and reduces immediate load).

Name: Use smart eviction policies
Guideline: Apply TTL, LRU, or LFU eviction so stale entries are removed and cache space stays available for the data that's actually being requested.
Context: The three policies serve slightly different goals: TTL expires data by age regardless of use, LRU evicts whatever hasn't been accessed most recently, and LFU evicts whatever's accessed least often overall — picking the one matching your actual access pattern is what keeps the cache full of genuinely hot data rather than stale leftovers.

Name: Focus on reducing complexity
Guideline: Evaluate an algorithm's theoretical time and space complexity, not just observed runtime, when choosing an approach that minimizes resource consumption.
Context: Google's concrete example: choosing merge sort over bubble sort for large datasets — a difference invisible on small test data but one that significantly changes computational load and energy consumption as the dataset actually scales up in production.

Name: Avoid redundant work
Guideline: Rely on built-in, language- or framework-optimized functions, typically implemented in efficient lower-level languages, instead of reimplementing common operations.
Context: Google's specific reasoning: built-in framework functions are typically implemented in lower-level, highly optimized languages like C or C++ under the hood, so even a seemingly-equivalent custom implementation in your application's own language usually runs less efficiently.

Name: Optimize for search and retrieval
Guideline: Use hash maps or hash sets for near-constant-time lookups instead of linear searches through arrays, cutting the energy spent per query.
Context: The efficiency gap here widens with scale: a linear search's energy cost grows proportionally with dataset size, while a hash map's near-constant-time lookup barely changes — meaning the payoff of this choice compounds as your data grows rather than staying fixed.

Name: Minimize memory footprint
Guideline: Choose compact, efficient data structures to shrink an application's memory usage, which lowers power consumption and delays the need for hardware upgrades.
Context: Beyond the direct power savings, Google frames a lower memory footprint as also delaying the point where more or larger hardware becomes necessary — an indirect embodied-carbon benefit on top of the immediate energy-consumption one.

Name: Use specialized structures
Guideline: Apply purpose-built structures, such as tries for prefix searches or priority queues for min/max access, when they fit the access pattern better than general-purpose collections.
Context: The general principle behind naming specific structures like tries and priority queues: a general-purpose collection like a plain list or array often does more work than necessary for a specialized access pattern, since it's paying the overhead of supporting operations your code never actually calls.

Name: Prefer event-driven logic over polling
Guideline: Replace busy-wait loops or periodic polling with event-driven triggers so processing only happens on demand.
Context: The core inefficiency polling has that event-driven logic avoids: a polling loop burns CPU cycles checking for a change even during long stretches where nothing has actually happened, while an event-driven trigger only runs code when there's genuinely something to process.

Name: Prevent constant high frequency
Guideline: Avoid code patterns that force the CPU to run continuously at maximum frequency, so idle systems can drop into low-power states.
Context: The specific mechanism: certain code patterns — like tight busy-wait loops — inadvertently prevent the CPU's own hardware power-management features from ever engaging, since the chip never sees the sustained idle gaps it needs to drop into a lower-power state.

Name: Use asynchronous processing
Guideline: Use async processing so threads aren't blocked waiting on I/O, freeing compute resources for other work and improving overall utilization.
Context: The specific waste this avoids: a thread blocked waiting on I/O still occupies scheduling and memory overhead even though it's doing no useful work in that moment — freeing it via async processing lets that capacity serve other requests instead of sitting idle-but-reserved.

Name: Strict memory management
Guideline: Proactively release memory that's no longer needed rather than holding large objects longer than necessary, to avoid resource bottlenecks.
Context: The downstream cost Google is pointing at: holding large objects in memory longer than necessary forces either a higher peak memory allocation or more garbage-collector work later to reclaim it — both of which carry their own energy cost beyond the memory footprint itself.

Name: Optimize disk I/O
Guideline: Buffer writes in memory and flush to persistent storage at set intervals or size thresholds rather than performing frequent small disk operations.
Context: The underlying reason buffering helps: each individual disk operation carries a fixed overhead cost regardless of how much data it moves, so batching many small writes into fewer, larger ones amortizes that fixed cost across more actual data per operation.

Name: Batch operations
Guideline: Consolidate many small disk reads and writes into fewer, larger batch operations, which consume less energy than numerous individual transactions.
Context: Where this differs from buffering writes in memory (a related guideline): batching is about the size of each transaction once you do write — combining what would be many small reads or writes into fewer, larger ones, which Google notes consumes less total energy than the same data moved via many individual small transactions.

Name: Use compression
Guideline: Apply suitable data-compression techniques, such as Cloud Storage's decompressive transcoding, to reduce the volume of data written to and read from disk.
Context: Google's concrete example is Cloud Storage's decompressive transcoding feature specifically — data can be stored compressed and served decompressed automatically, getting the storage/transfer savings without the application itself needing to handle the compression logic.

Name: Minimize payload size
Guideline: Design APIs and applications to transfer only the fields a request actually needs, avoiding oversized JSON or XML payloads.
Context: The specific anti-pattern this targets: an API endpoint returning an entire object's worth of fields when the calling code only actually reads one or two of them — designing the response shape around actual field usage avoids that unnecessary transfer.

Name: Reduce round-trips
Guideline: Adopt more efficient protocols and patterns -- HTTP/3 over HTTP/1.1, GraphQL over REST, binary protocols, and consolidated API calls -- to cut the number of network round-trips.
Context: Similar reasoning to batching disk operations: each network round-trip carries its own fixed overhead independent of how much data it carries, so consolidating several calls into one (or switching to a protocol like HTTP/3 that handles multiplexing more efficiently) cuts that fixed per-trip cost rather than just the data volume.

Name: Minimization and compression
Guideline: Strip unnecessary characters from JavaScript, CSS, and HTML with minification tools, and compress images and other assets as part of the CI/CD pipeline.
Context: Google's specific recommendation is to automate this via the CI/CD pipeline rather than relying on developers to manually minify and compress assets before each deploy — treating it as a build step everyone gets by default, not an opt-in practice.

Name: Lazy loading
Guideline: Load images, videos, and other non-critical assets only when they're about to be needed, such as when scrolled into view, to cut initial data transfer.
Context: The same underlying logic as caching applied to page load specifically: content below the fold that a visitor may never actually scroll to shouldn't cost anything on initial load, since there's a real chance that data transfer and rendering work never needed to happen at all.

Name: Smaller JavaScript bundles
Guideline: Use modern bundlers and tree shaking to strip unused code out of JavaScript bundles, producing smaller, faster-loading files.
Context: A small per-visit saving here compounds significantly at scale: shaving even a modest amount off a JavaScript bundle gets multiplied by every single page load across every visitor, which is why bundle size specifically gets called out as worth this level of attention.

Name: Browser caching
Guideline: Set HTTP caching headers so browsers store static assets locally, avoiding repeated downloads and unnecessary network traffic on return visits.
Context: This specifically benefits return visitors rather than first-time ones: HTTP caching headers tell the browser it can reuse a previously-downloaded asset instead of re-fetching it, so the saving compounds the more often the same person comes back to the site.

Name: Efficient rendering
Guideline: Minimize frequent DOM manipulation and unnecessary re-rendering to keep client-side rendering lightweight.
Context: A common source of the waste this targets: state changes in reactive frameworks that trigger a re-render even though the actual visible output hasn't changed — minimizing unnecessary DOM manipulation means also avoiding renders that were never going to change anything on screen.

Name: Lightweight design patterns
Guideline: Favor static sites or progressive web apps over heavier dynamic architectures, since they load faster and need fewer server resources.
Context: The contrast this is drawn against: a fully dynamic architecture that regenerates a page fresh on every single request, when a static site or PWA could serve the same (or cached) content without repeating that server-side work each time nothing has actually changed.

Name: Accessibility and performance
Guideline: Build responsive, fast-loading, accessible sites, since accessible design and lean performance typically go hand in hand with lower resource consumption.
Context: Google cites a concrete figure to make the business case alongside the sustainability one: a 0.1-second page-speed improvement is associated with an 8.4% increase in retail conversions in cited research — the same lightweight, clutter-free design serving both goals at once.

Name: Identify and eliminate duplication
Guideline: Set policies against needless dataset replication, using centralized, access-controlled repositories as the single source of truth.
Context: Google's concrete example of what a "centralized repository" means in practice: a BigQuery dataset or a Cloud Storage bucket designated as the single source of truth, rather than each team or project keeping its own separately-synced copy.

Name: Remove shadow data and dark data
Guideline: Use discovery tooling to find unauthorized copies and data of unknown value, then archive or delete it appropriately.
Context: Google's concrete tool for this discovery step is Knowledge Catalog, used to scan storage systems and surface copies and datasets whose ownership or purpose isn't documented, before deciding whether to archive or delete them.

Name: Minimize the data volume for AI workloads
Guideline: Use sampling, aggregation, and synthetic data generation to keep model performance while avoiding storage of unnecessarily large raw datasets.
Context: The framing Google gives is explicitly a tradeoff, not a blanket cut: the goal is finding the point where sampling, aggregation, or synthetic data generation still preserves the model performance you need, rather than minimizing data volume at any accuracy cost.

Name: Integrate data quality checks
Guideline: Run automated validation and cleaning pipelines at ingestion so low-quality data doesn't waste storage and energy downstream.
Context: Google names the concrete tools for this: Managed Service for Apache Spark, Dataflow, or Knowledge Catalog, applied specifically at the point of data ingestion — catching low-quality data before it's stored is what avoids paying the storage and processing cost for data that turns out not to be usable anyway.

Name: Review the value density of data
Guideline: Periodically assess high-volume datasets, like logs and IoT streams, to see whether aggregation or down-sampling can preserve useful information while shrinking storage footprint.
Context: Google frames this as a periodic review rather than a one-time design decision: as data volume and usage patterns shift over time, a dataset that once justified full-resolution storage may later be safely summarized or down-sampled without losing the information anyone actually still uses.

Name: Critically evaluate the need for backups
Guideline: Keep backups only for data that is unique or expensive to recreate, and avoid retaining copies of easily regenerated data such as intermediate ETL output or ephemeral caches.
Context: Google's concrete examples of data that typically doesn't need backing up: intermediate ETL results, ephemeral caches, and derived training data — all things that can be regenerated from an earlier stage in the pipeline rather than needing their own backup copy.

Name: Select an appropriate Cloud Storage class
Guideline: Automate transitions of data to lower-carbon storage classes, such as Archive, based on how frequently it's accessed.
Context: Google names the concrete storage-class tiers to move data through as access frequency drops — Standard, Nearline, Coldline, then Archive — automated via Cloud Storage's Object Lifecycle Management rather than requiring someone to manually reclassify data as it ages.

Name: Implement aggressive data lifecycle policies
Guideline: Define automated time-to-live rules for non-essential data such as logs and temporary artifacts so it's deleted automatically after a set period.
Context: Distinct from moving data to cheaper storage tiers (a related guideline): this is about outright automated deletion once data crosses an age threshold — the two are complementary, since not every dataset needs to be kept at all, even in cold storage.

Name: Mandate resource tagging
Guideline: Require consistent labels on storage resources for ownership, purpose, and retention period, enabling automated lifecycle management and emissions reporting.
Context: Google's concrete enforcement mechanism: an Organization Policy constraint that requires these tags at resource-creation time, rather than relying on teams to remember to tag things voluntarily after the fact — which is what makes the tags reliable enough to actually automate lifecycle management and reporting from.

Name: Right-size and deprovision compute storage
Guideline: Regularly audit persistent disks for overprovisioning, delete unneeded snapshots, and apply retention policies to shrink underlying storage requirements.
Context: This guideline specifically targets compute-attached storage — persistent disks and their snapshots — as distinct from object storage lifecycle policies covered elsewhere, since disk over-provisioning and forgotten snapshots are a common, easy-to-overlook source of storage waste specific to VM-based workloads.

Name: Optimize the storage format
Guideline: Use compressed, columnar formats such as Parquet instead of row-based formats to cut disk-space use and improve read efficiency.
Context: Google names Parquet as the primary recommendation but also allows for optimized Avro as an alternative — both are columnar or column-friendly formats that read and compress more efficiently than row-based formats like CSV for analytics workloads specifically.

Name: Select low-carbon storage regions
Guideline: Store data in regions with cleaner grids, and use Organization Policy constraints to prevent resource creation in high-carbon locations.
Context: This applies the same Organization Policy mechanism used for compute region selection, but to storage bucket creation specifically — so a team can't accidentally spin up a data store in a high-carbon region even if they never think to check the region's carbon profile themselves.

Name: Minimize replication
Guideline: Replicate data across regions only when required for disaster recovery or high availability, since cross-region replication meaningfully increases energy cost.
Context: The practical target here is often a default setting: some storage services replicate across regions by default for convenience, and this pattern is about deliberately opting out of that default wherever genuine disaster-recovery or high-availability requirements don't actually apply.

Name: Optimize data processing locations
Guideline: Run compute-intensive processing in the same region as the data it reads to avoid the energy cost of unnecessary cross-region network transfer.
Context: Google's concrete examples of the compute-intensive workloads this matters most for: AI training jobs and BigQuery processing specifically, both of which move substantial data volume and so benefit the most from running in the same region the data already lives in.

Name: Optimize data movement for your partners and customers
Guideline: Direct partners toward efficient transfer methods like Storage Transfer Service and consider Requester Pays buckets so the environmental cost of transfers is attributed appropriately.
Context: The Requester Pays mechanism Google points to does something specific: it shifts both the cost and, implicitly, the accountability for a transfer's environmental impact onto whichever partner or customer is actually requesting the data, rather than the data owner absorbing it by default.

Name: Grant permissions
Guideline: Grant relevant teams the Carbon Footprint Viewer IAM role so they can access carbon emissions data in the Google Cloud console.
Context: The exact IAM role name is `roles/billing.carbonViewer` — a specific, minimal permission scoped just to viewing carbon data, rather than requiring broader billing-account access to get teams looking at emissions data.

Name: Automate data export
Guideline: Structure the resource hierarchy to reflect business units and configure automated exports of Carbon Footprint data to BigQuery for deeper analysis and custom reporting.
Context: Google is explicit about sequencing: the resource hierarchy and labeling has to be accurate before the export is useful, since the BigQuery data will only be as well-organized by business unit as the underlying project structure it's drawn from.

Name: Define carbon-related key performance indicators (KPIs)
Guideline: Establish metrics that connect emissions to business value, such as CO2e per customer, transaction, or revenue unit.
Context: The reason for tying carbon to a business unit like per-customer or per-transaction, rather than tracking a raw total: it lets you tell genuine efficiency improvement apart from growth — a rising total emissions number could still mean falling carbon intensity per unit of actual business delivered.

Name: Prioritize by scope
Guideline: Break down Carbon Footprint data by project, region, and service to quickly find the largest sources of emissions.
Context: The point of this breakdown specifically is triage: finding the handful of projects, regions, or services responsible for a disproportionate share of emissions is what tells you where an optimization effort will actually move the needle, rather than reviewing every resource with equal priority.

Name: Use dual-accounting
Guideline: Evaluate regional carbon impact using both location-based emissions from the local grid and market-based emissions that reflect Google's carbon-free energy purchases.
Context: The two accounting methods can genuinely disagree for the same region — a location that's carbon-intensive on the local grid can still look better market-based if Google has purchased enough carbon-free energy there — so Google recommends looking at both rather than picking whichever number happens to look better.

Name: Correlate with cost
Guideline: Join carbon and billing data in BigQuery so optimization decisions can weigh sustainability and cost together rather than cost alone.
Context: The practical reason for joining these datasets: an optimization can genuinely save carbon while increasing cost, or the reverse, and without looking at both together a team might unknowingly optimize for one at the other's expense.

Name: Annotate data to measure return on effort (ROE)
Guideline: Tag carbon data with specific optimization events, such as a right-sizing change, so the resulting emissions reduction can be attributed to that action.
Context: This is what turns a general downward trend in the emissions dashboard into causal attribution for a specific action — without the annotation, you'd see carbon go down sometime after a right-sizing change but have no rigorous way to credit that change specifically versus other factors.

Name: Decommission unattended projects
Guideline: Use the unattended-project recommender alongside Carbon Footprint data to find and remove unused projects for immediate, verifiable emissions reduction.
Context: The recommender for this is built directly into the Carbon Footprint data itself, rather than requiring a separate manual audit process — so identifying an abandoned project and quantifying its associated emissions happen through the same tool rather than two disconnected steps.

Name: Right-size resources
Guideline: Apply Active Assist recommendations to match provisioned capacity to actual utilization, including choosing more efficient machine types for compute- and AI-heavy workloads.
Context: Active Assist is Google's broader family of automated recommenders that this pattern draws on — machine-type right-sizing for Compute Engine is the specific example named here, but the same underlying recommender system covers several of the other optimization patterns in this framework too.

Name: Adopt carbon-aware scheduling
Guideline: For batch workloads without strict timing needs, factor regional carbon-free energy data into scheduling and use Organization Policy to restrict new resources to low-carbon regions.
Context: Like the storage and region guidelines elsewhere in this framework, the enforcement mechanism here is the same Organization Policy constraint restricting new resources to low-carbon regions — applied here specifically to batch scheduling decisions rather than a one-time resource-creation choice.

Name: Reduce data sprawl
Guideline: Apply data governance to move infrequently accessed data to cold storage or delete it outright, cutting storage-related energy use.
Context: This is the measurement-side counterpart to the storage-optimization guidelines elsewhere in the framework: where those cover the mechanics of tiering and deletion, this one is about using carbon and usage data specifically to identify which sprawling datasets are worth that treatment in the first place.

Name: Refine application code
Guideline: Address code-level inefficiencies that cause excessive resource use or unnecessary computation.
Context: Google’s framework places this in its "continuously measure and improve" phase: after spotting inefficient workloads through monitoring, refactor the code itself — not just the infrastructure — since application-level waste shows up directly as extra compute and carbon footprint.

Name: Implement GreenOps governance
Guideline: Stand up a formal function that combines Carbon Footprint and Cloud Billing data in shared dashboards, embedding sustainability into regular operational reviews.
Context: Google's concrete example of where this data lands operationally is a FinOps dashboard tool like Looker — the point being GreenOps isn't a separate reporting silo but gets folded into the same operational review process and tooling that already exists for cost management.

Name: Use Carbon Footprint data for reporting and compliance
Guideline: Use Google's verified, auditable carbon data to support ESG disclosures and other stakeholder transparency requirements.
Context: The specific property that makes this usable for external ESG disclosure, rather than just internal tracking, is that the data is verified and auditable — a distinction that matters once the numbers are going into a public or regulatory filing rather than staying inside the team.

Name: Invest in training and awareness
Guideline: Provide mandatory training so teams can access, interpret, and act on carbon data and optimization recommendations in their daily work.
Context: Google frames this as something teams apply routinely in their daily work — interpreting carbon data and acting on optimization recommendations as a standing practice — rather than a one-time onboarding session that's never revisited once the training is complete.

Name: Define carbon requirements
Guideline: Add carbon-emission metrics as non-functional requirements in application acceptance criteria so low-carbon design is considered from the start of development.
Context: Framing carbon as a non-functional requirement — the same category as latency or availability targets — means it can actually gate a release the way those do, rather than being something measured and reported on only after the system is already live.

Name: Automate GreenOps
Guideline: Use scripts, templates, and infrastructure-as-code to automatically apply Active Assist recommendations consistently across the organization.
Context: The specific value of automating this: applying Active Assist recommendations manually, project by project, doesn't scale across a large organization — scripting or templating the application means a recommendation gets acted on consistently everywhere it applies, not just wherever someone happened to review it by hand.

Name: Connect to the big picture
Guideline: Help teams see how their architectural choices contribute to the organization's sustainability commitments, turning abstract carbon metrics into tangible progress indicators.
Context: Google gives a concrete worked example for making this tangible: a workload migration to a low-carbon region cited as achieving a 75% reduction in carbon intensity and roughly 12 metric tons of CO2 equivalent saved per quarter — the kind of specific number that makes "sustainability progress" concrete rather than abstract.

Name: Communicate financial and sustainability goals
Guideline: Share sustainability objectives and progress transparently across the organization, including in financial reporting, so technical teams see their work as tied to public commitments.
Context: Google's specific recommendation extends beyond internal communication: highlighting sustainability progress in the organization's actual annual financial statements is called out specifically, tying the technical work to a public, board-level commitment rather than keeping it as an internal engineering metric.

Name: Embrace a shared fate mindset
Guideline: Teach teams that Google manages the sustainability of the underlying cloud infrastructure while customers manage the sustainability of their own workloads, framing it as a shared partnership.
Context: This mirrors the standard cloud shared-responsibility security model applied to sustainability instead: Google's side of the line is the infrastructure itself, and everything a customer builds and runs on top of it is the customer's side — the guideline is about making that division explicit to teams rather than assuming it's obvious.

Name: Provide role-based sustainability training
Guideline: Tailor sustainability education by role -- compute intensity for data scientists, code efficiency for developers, region selection for architects, utilization for operations, and strategic alignment for leadership.
Context: Google's concrete example for one of these roles: architects specifically get trained on region selection, citing a low-carbon region like northamerica-northeast1 as the kind of specific, actionable knowledge that role-based training should convey rather than generic sustainability awareness.

Name: Empower managers to advocate for sustainability
Guideline: Give managers the data and authority to weigh environmental impact alongside business metrics, so they can champion greener infrastructure choices.
Context: Google's specific framing: managers should be able to weigh environmental impact with the same decision-making authority they already have over metrics like speed-to-market and cost — not a special separate process requiring extra approval, but folded into the same everyday tradeoffs.

Name: Align with industry standards and frameworks
Guideline: Ground sustainability efforts in recognized global and regional standards to keep them credible and measurable.
Context: The specific purpose Google names for this: aligning with recognized external standards is what keeps your sustainability claims credible to outside stakeholders, rather than risking the appearance of having invented internal metrics favorable to your own story.

Name: Define carbon KPIs and NFRs
Guideline: Set specific, measurable sustainability targets, such as CO2 per request or per training run, and treat them as core technical requirements alongside latency and availability.
Context: Where this differs from making carbon an acceptance-criteria requirement (a related guideline): this is about setting the target itself — a specific number like grams of CO2 equivalent per million requests — as an organizational goal, which the acceptance-criteria practice then enforces project by project.

Name: Measure return on effort
Guideline: Help teams find high-impact, low-effort sustainability improvements by giving visibility into carbon avoided relative to the effort required.
Context: This adds an effort dimension to the prioritization question: it's not just about finding where emissions are largest, but about finding where a given amount of effort yields the most carbon avoided — which might favor a simple win over a technically larger but far more complex refactor.

Name: Recognize and celebrate carbon reduction
Guideline: Make sustainability wins visible across the organization through dashboards and recognition, to build momentum for continued progress.
Context: The mechanism Google names ties back to the data-annotation practice elsewhere in this framework: annotating the monitoring dashboard at the moment a team deploys a sustainability optimization is what lets that team's specific contribution be recognized and celebrated, rather than an anonymous improvement in an aggregate number.

Name: W3C Web Sustainability Guidelines
Guideline: Follow the W3C Web Sustainability Guidelines to build more energy-efficient websites and applications across the full lifecycle, from business strategy to infrastructure, reducing network traffic, client processing, and server load.
Context: This is Google's own framework pointing back to the same W3C Web Sustainability Guidelines already covered as their own separate source in this dataset — Google frames WSG as still an emerging framework rather than a finalized standard, covering everything from business strategy down to infrastructure choices.

Name: Green Software Foundation
Guideline: Adopt the Green Software Foundation's Software Carbon Intensity (SCI) specification as a common standard for measuring a software system's carbon emissions rate.
Context: This is the same Green Software Foundation whose Patterns Catalog is covered as its own source elsewhere in this dataset — the SCI specification it developed is the measurement standard several of those individual patterns explicitly tie their guidance back to (the Energy and embodied-carbon terms referenced throughout that source's context notes).

Name: Greenhouse Gas Protocol
Guideline: Report emissions using the GHG Protocol, the widely adopted WRI/WBCSD standard for measuring, managing, and publicly disclosing greenhouse gas emissions, to keep sustainability data credible and auditable.
Context: This is the same accounting framework underlying the location-based-versus-market-based emissions distinction covered elsewhere in this source (GCP.MEASURE.5) — the GHG Protocol is what defines those two methods, not something GCP invented for its own carbon reporting.
